opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the problem is that the very framing assumes you can pull apart two separate ingredients and ask how much of each went into the cake. But development doesn't work like that. What we've learned from developmental biology and from studying children is that the "nature" part, the genetic and evolutionary inheritance, is itself a program for being shaped by experience. And the experience part is structured by what the organism brings to it.

Think about human beings specifically. Our nature is to have an exceptionally long childhood, a long period of protected immaturity in which we're surrounded by caregivers who invest an enormous amount in us. That's an evolved feature of our species, absolutely part of our nature. But what it's *for* is to let us learn, to let culture and the particular environment we're in shape us. So it's our nature to be nurtured. Asking which part is innate and which is learned is a bit like asking whether a computer's output comes from the hardware or the software.

There's also a more technical point. Even with something that looks heavily heritable, the heritability estimate only tells you about variation within a particular range of environments. Change the environment and the numbers change. So the idea that there's a fixed percentage that's "genetic" is really an illusion of the specific circumstances you happened to measure.

And from the perspective of the child, what's striking is how actively they construct their understanding of the world. Babies and young children are like little scientists: they come equipped with powerful learning mechanisms, ways of forming hypotheses, testing them, and revising them in light of evidence. Those mechanisms are innate in some sense, but what they produce depends completely on the data the child encounters. The interesting question isn't "how much is nature versus nurture," it's "what are the learning mechanisms, and how do they interact with the environment to produce this extraordinary flexibility?"

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that it's not really a dichotomy at all, and the people who actually study development have known that for a long time. If you look at what's actually going on in a developing brain, or a developing organism, what you see is that the genes are, in effect, designed to extract information from the environment. So the question "how much is nature and how much is nurture" is a bit like asking how much of the area of a rectangle comes from its length and how much from its width. It just isn't a well-formed question.

But I think there's something deeper than that too, which is that when people say "nature," they tend to imagine a kind of fixed blueprint, and when they say "nurture," they imagine a blank slate being written on by experience. And neither of those is what evolution actually produced. What evolution produced, especially in human beings, is a system that's designed to learn. Children come into the world with very powerful learning mechanisms — the ability to do something like Bayesian inference, the ability to do little experiments, the ability to pick up information from other people — and those are innate in the sense that every child has them. But what they're innate for is precisely to let the child change in response to what's out there. So the most important thing that's in our nature is our capacity to be shaped by nurture.

And then the other piece, which I think people often miss, is that children aren't just passive recipients of either their genes or their environment. They're actively going out and getting the information they need. A two-year-old who's taking apart the remote control is doing science, and the environment they're in is partly an environment they've created. So you've got this very complicated causal loop where the child's genes influence the kind of environment the child seeks out, that environment changes the child, and the changed child seeks out something different. Once you see it that way, trying to carve the whole thing into two neat piles just stops making sense.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the problem is that it suggests that there are two separate ingredients, and you could figure out how much of development comes from each one. But what we know about development is that it’s a process in which genes and environments are continually interacting. The genes help shape how an organism responds to its environment, and the environment helps shape which genes get expressed.

Learning is a particularly good example. People sometimes talk as if saying that something is learned means that it isn’t innate. But our capacity to learn is itself one of the most important things that evolution has given us. You need a lot of innate structure to be able to learn as much as a human child does.

And children aren’t just passively receiving environmental influences. They’re exploring, experimenting, choosing what to pay attention to, and changing the responses of the people around them. So the interesting question isn’t, “Is this nature or nurture?” It’s, “What are the processes that allow this particular child, in this particular environment, to develop in this particular way?”

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the problem is that nature and nurture aren’t two separate ingredients that you can measure independently and then add together. Development is a process in which what an organism inherits shapes how it interacts with its environment, and those interactions shape what the organism becomes.

Learning is a good example. We sometimes talk as if something is either innate or learned. But our capacity to learn is itself part of our biological inheritance. You can have an immensely powerful innate learning system that produces very different outcomes depending on what experience it encounters.

So the useful question isn’t, “How much is nature and how much is nurture?” It’s, “What are the mechanisms by which this particular organism, in this particular environment, develops?” That’s a much more informative question, although it’s also a harder one.
